title: How can we motivate our students?
author: Jo Castelino
summary: Jo Castelino, a secondary science teacher, sets out classroom techniques for motivating students who give up at the first sign of challenge, drawing on Peps McCrea's Motivated Teaching. She argues that motivation grows from students seeing that effort is worth their time, not from making lessons fun. Her techniques include sharing annotated exemplars and building toward Show Call once classroom culture is respectful, deliberately building belonging by sharing strategies and resources, and making the payoff of effort immediate through small successes such as self-quizzing. She adds remote-teaching variants using Loom videos and voice-note feedback. She ends with a plan for the return to the classroom, noting students' small successes and contacting home for those who could not engage remotely.
points: Exemplars and Show Call work best once the classroom culture is respectful, so the teacher should build up to public critique rather than start there.
Belonging comes from explicitly showing students what hard work looks like and letting them hear how peers solved difficult problems.
Motivation for under-confident students needs immediate, visible benefits, such as noticing that self-quizzing makes the same questions easier, rather than distant targets like exams.
Personal touches such as voice-note feedback and contacting home help students who struggle with confidence.
Castelino plans to record small successes for fragile students and refer to them subtly when they say they cannot do something.

The answer to this does not lie in making lessons fun (read more about what I think about fun and games) but in helping students see that in our classroom we work hard and do our best. Just saying this and displaying it on a laminated sheet won’t do the trick. We need to believe it and explicitly show students what hard work looks like, how they can achieve success, and what they must do to overcome problems.
If a student hears how their peers were able to answer a difficult question using appropriate resources, it gives them ideas for what to do when stuck in the future instead of giving up.
Instead of focusing on a far-off target such as their GCSE exams or using a bit of Science one day in life, it is important to make some benefits more obvious and immediate.
For instance, when they self-quiz from a list of key core questions, they will find that answering the same questions becomes easier with time. This may seem like a distant target to some

I have also been using Mote (a Google add-on that allows me to record voice messages) to provide feedback to students, which makes it more personal than a typed message. I don’t use this for every student every time but I do try to ensure some feedback is provided verbally using my own voice, particularly for those students that struggle with motivation and confidence. It means that students hear their own teacher telling them something rather than reading the same thing.
